title: Petrillo and Gray's agreement and why 208 wanted to merge
summary: They discuss the Petrillo-Gray understanding that kept the locals apart and why Local 208 members voted unanimously to merge: death benefit, taxes and better contracts.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, the story is that Petrillo and Gray were both presidents of the respective locals for many years.
Had this agreement that there would not be an integration of the --
Right. Well, they were trying to preserve the dynasty for the black officials. See, that was
what this was. That was a real fight. The real fight was preserving the dynasty for the black officials, and then the white officials would -- they didn't want to bring them together.
It wasn't the musicians who resisted integration.

No, no, they had a vote. They had a vote and it was unanimous to merge, from 208. 208 had a vote and it was really unanimous that they wanted to merge. Because in 208 we had a $500 death benefit, so they would get -- it was $1,000 at that time. So that meant $500 more on the death benefit.

Here we were paying four percent tax and there you were paying two percent tax. So that was another plus in saving of money. And then, the better jobs -- they had contracts, 10 had contracts with the radio stations for the disc jockeys and the blah-blah-blah, and the different auditoriums and things like that. They had contracts with these.
So in order -- so automatically you were closed out, although you were supposed to have the same working conditions.
